subject: anaesthesia
title: History of Anaesthesia, Medical Gas Cylinders, and Pipeline Safety

steps.title: William Morton Ether Demonstration
steps.tx: **William Morton ether demonstration** on October 16, 1846, at the Ether Dome of Massachusetts General Hospital marks the birth of modern surgical anaesthesia. Morton administered diethyl ether via an inhaler to patient Gilbert Abbott, allowing surgeon John Collins Warren to painlessly excise a neck vascular tumour. Following the successful procedure, Warren famously declared to the audience: 'Gentlemen, this is no humbug.'

steps.title: John Snow and Chloroform Inhalers
steps.tx: **John Snow epidemiological and anaesthetic legacy** established him as the world first dedicated full-time specialist anaesthetist. Snow constructed calibrated temperature-compensated chloroform vaporizers to eliminate lethal overdoses, authored the first scientific textbook on inhalational anaesthesia, and safely administered chloroform to Queen Victoria during the births of Prince Leopold in 1853 and Princess Beatrice in 1857.

steps.title: Medical Gas Cylinder Colour Coding
steps.tx: **Medical gas cylinder colour coding** prevents lethal cylinder mix-ups: under International Organization for Standardization (ISO) guidelines, medical oxygen cylinders have a black body with a white shoulder (pure white in updated ISO; green in United States), nitrous oxide cylinders are painted French blue, medical air is grey with black and white quartered shoulders, carbon dioxide is grey, and helium is brown.

steps.title: Entonox Composition and Properties
steps.tx: **Entonox cylinder composition** contains an exact 50:50 mixture of compressed medical oxygen and nitrous oxide under 137 bar pressure, housed in cylinders with a French blue body and white-and-blue quartered shoulders. If cooled below its pseudocritical temperature of minus 5.5 degrees Celsius, the gases separate (Poynting effect), causing pure liquid nitrous oxide to settle at the bottom, risking delivery of an anoxic mixture unless re-warmed and inverted.

steps.title: Pin Index Safety System
steps.tx: **Pin Index Safety System geometry** incorporates specific pin configurations on the anaesthesia machine yoke that must match mating holes drilled into the cylinder valve body. This mechanical geometric keying prevents accidental mounting of incorrect gas cylinders: oxygen uses pin positions 2 and 5, nitrous oxide uses pins 3 and 5, medical air uses pins 1 and 5, and Entonox uses single pin position 7.

steps.title: Cylinder Pressure and Physical State
steps.tx: **Physical state inside cylinders** governs how cylinder pressure gauges behave: oxygen is a non-liquefied permanent gas, meaning cylinder pressure decreases linearly in direct proportion to contents, so a 2,000 psi gauge reading half-pressure (1,000 psi) confirms the cylinder is exactly 50 percent full. In contrast, nitrous oxide exists as a liquid in equilibrium with vapor at 750 psi; its pressure gauge remains fixed at 750 psi until all liquid vaporizes, after which pressure drops precipitously.

left.title: Oxygen Cylinder Monitoring
points: Direct linear correlation between pressure and gas volume
Boyle law applies directly across all temperatures
Pressure gauge reliably reflects remaining gas volume

right.title: Nitrous Oxide Cylinder Monitoring
points: Gauge stays constant at 750 psi while liquid remains
Pressure drops only when last drop of liquid evaporates
Weighing tare weight is the only accurate measure of contents

steps.title: Bodok Seal and Yoke Assembly
steps.tx: **Bodok seal gasket integrity** is vital when mounting cylinders onto the anaesthesia machine hanger yoke. The Bodok seal is a non-combustible neoprene rubber washer bonded to a brass or aluminium ring, designed to withstand high pressure up to 137 bar. It guarantees a gas-tight seal between the cylinder valve face and yoke nipple, preventing dangerous high-pressure gas leaks and fire hazards from escaping compressed oxygen.

steps.title: Vacuum Insulated Evaporator
steps.tx: **Liquid oxygen vacuum insulated evaporator** serves large hospitals as the primary bulk storage system, storing liquid oxygen at minus 160 to minus 183 degrees Celsius inside a double-walled stainless-steel container separated by perlite insulation under high vacuum. Because liquid oxygen expands 860 times into gas at ambient room temperature, a single compact VIE tank provides continuous high-purity oxygen at 4.1 bar pipeline pressure.
